A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete, readable 19-page versions of the same HIDDENBENCH paper. Text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison; Appendices A.1–A.4 are unchanged.

before.justification: v3 reports original LLM benchmark and ablation results, plus human experiments involving 96 participants described in Appendix A.3 and analyzed in Section 3.2.

after.justification: v4 retains the original human and LLM experiments and reports expanded diagnostic studies and a new structured communication experiment in Sections 6.2–6.4.

M1.justification: New Section 6.4 introduces an Exchange-then-Decide communication procedure: two rounds of sharing decision-relevant facts and challenging the leading option, followed by evidence and uncertainty summaries before voting. This adds a substantive coordination mechanism beyond v3's dissent, disclosure, and summarization interventions.

E1.justification: The 65-task benchmark, human-study scenarios, and group-size task variants remain. The expanded diagnostic experiments sample existing HIDDENBENCH tasks; the real-world examples added in Section 3.1 motivate applicability without adding evaluated domains or task requirements.

E2.justification: The main benchmark model roster and existing comparison procedures remain. Table 5 retains the same dissent compositions, and Table 6 retains Baseline, Reveal-All, and Secretary. Additional model backbones expand the experimental settings; the new proposed protocol is compared against the existing unstructured baseline.

E3.justification: Table 6 replaces the three-task GPT-4.1 evaluation with 18 tasks, comprising three manually crafted and 15 randomly sampled tasks, evaluated using GPT-4.1 and Gemini-2.5-Flash. Table 5 expands to five model backbones. Section 6.4 adds a four-agent, three-model evaluation on the same 18-task sample.

E4.justification: Dissent sensitivity is investigated across five models instead of GPT-4.1 alone, and disclosure versus summarization receives broader testing. New Section 6.4 tests whether the diagnosed failures can guide an effective communication intervention without explicitly revealing information asymmetry or forcing complete disclosure.

E5.justification: The reported ± uncertainty values disappear from Tables 5–6, and new Table 7 reports only point estimates. Section 6.4 specifies five runs per task for its new experiment. Existing benchmark session counts, Figure 3 standard errors, and verification significance tests remain; this does not establish reduced runs for retained experiments.

E6.justification: Table 5 retains GPT-4.1 mean accuracies and adds four models' results. Table 6 replaces three-task GPT-4.1 baseline/Reveal-All/Secretary accuracies of 0.233/0.967/0.100 with 18-task values of 0.037/0.926/0.241, so these are not same-setting performance changes. New Table 7 reports structured accuracies of 0.800, 0.727, and 0.743 for GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5-Flash, and Flash-Lite, alongside baselines of 0.037, 0.173, and 0.043.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2's information partitions, decision functions, aggregation rules, and Hidden Profile conditions are unchanged. Added conceptual motivation and removal of the introduction's informal policy-misalignment statement do not change formal reasoning or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's new fourth contribution, and conclusion explicitly add the claim that HIDDENBENCH can guide a practical communication protocol that substantially improves collective reasoning. This expands the central contribution beyond the retained benchmark and failure diagnosis.

C2.justification: Section 6.2 replaces the broadly presented Goldilocks interpretation with model-dependent effects, including harmful dissent for Gemini-2.5-Flash. Section 6.3 replaces the specific inference that ineffective summarization rules out forgetting with an interpretation acknowledging model-dependent summarization benefits and integration ability. Section 3.1 also adds an argument for real-world applicability without new real-world evaluation.

D1.justification: Section 4 replaces the anonymous repository link with named GitHub and Hugging Face links for the benchmark, evaluation suite, and generated corpus. Section 4.2 clarifies threshold averaging, and a new footnote explains that Reveal-All mechanically appends facts to first-round messages. These clarify existing implementation rather than establish procedural changes.

R1.justification: Sections 2–3 add connections to multitask transfer, distributed knowledge, transactive memory, and real-world coordination, citing works including Wu et al., Fagin et al., and Wegner. Pathak et al. and Dibangoye and Buffet are removed. The central positioning of HIDDENBENCH relative to previous evaluations remains.

P1.justification: Several introduction, benchmark-motivation, interpretation, and conclusion paragraphs are rewritten. Section 6.4 and acknowledgements are added, and affiliation ordering and publication-header text change. The overall section sequence and all appendix text remain substantially stable.

P2.justification: Tables 5–6 are restructured to display results across models, Table 7 is added, and existing tables shift within the ablation section. The three figures and Table 1 retain their displays, and the basic document layout remains unchanged.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens the central diagnostic evidence: previously narrow GPT-4.1 ablations gain broader model testing and an 18-task bottleneck evaluation, revealing exceptions that qualify the earlier interpretations. Section 6.4 also demonstrates a practical intervention without forced disclosure, strengthening the benchmark's usefulness. Clearer implementation explanations and resource links help reproducibility. Removing uncertainty from Tables 5–6 and omitting it from Table 7 weakens statistical reporting, but the broader, better-qualified evidence and constructive validation provide a substantial net improvement.
